title: The era of "legitimate trade" and colonial empires
competency: Explain the "legitimate trade", the infrastructure and ideology of the New Imperialism, and the motives and process of the partition of Africa.

keywords.def: The name for the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade, because the goods sold were human beings.
The 19th-century trade that replaced the slave trade in West Africa: gum, groundnuts and palm produce for European goods.
The policy of a strong state controlling other lands and peoples; the book calls it "the highest stage of capitalism".
The period of rapid European colonial expansion from the second half of the 19th century to the First World War (1914).
An area where one power claims special rights and keeps rivals out.
The rush of European powers to claim African land, slow in the 1870s and fastest after 1885.
Protecting a country's own trade and markets instead of free trade, for example by holding colonies.
The rule of one country over another people and land, to control and use them.

en.text: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade was called the "illegitimate trade" because its goods were human beings. After the Industrial Revolution Britain led its abolition, and Europeans started a "legitimate trade" in West African gum, groundnuts and palm produce; palm oil was the main export by the mid-19th century. It enriched rulers and wealthy merchants, not ordinary people, and imported cloth, alcohol and old firearms damaged local crafts. Competition among European merchants led to the Scramble for Africa.

am.text: የባሪያ ንግድ "ሕገወጥ ንግድ" ተባለ፤ በምትኩ የዘንባባ ዘይት፣ ለውዝና ሙጫ "ሕጋዊ ንግድ" ተጀመረ። የጠቀመው ገዢዎችንና ሀብታም ነጋዴዎችን ብቻ ነው።

ideas.name: The New Imperialism: tools and ideas

en.text: New Imperialism is the period of rapid capitalist expansion from the second half of the 19th century to the First World War (1914). Newly united Germany and Italy joined Britain and France, and a financial crisis in the early 1870s pushed the powers to protect their interests, for example by dividing West Africa into spheres of influence. Better river boats, steamships, rifles and medicine against malaria let small European armies enter the interior. By 1914 about 85 % of the world's territory was under colonial rule; in Africa only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed free.

am.text: አዲሱ ኢምፔሪያሊዝም ከ19ኛው ክፍለ ዘመን አጋማሽ እስከ 1914 ነው። የተሻሉ መርከቦች፣ ጠመንጃዎችና የወባ መድኃኒት አውሮፓውያን ወደ አፍሪካ ውስጥ እንዲገቡ አስቻሉ። ኢትዮጵያና ላይቤሪያ ብቻ ነፃ ቀሩ።

ideas.name: Motives for the Scramble for Africa

en.text: By the 1870s industrial Western Europe was the most powerful continent. An economic decline in the early 1870s made Europeans see Africa as a market for their goods and a source of raw materials; national pride and fear for the balance of power added to this. Britain, the leading industrial nation with the largest merchant navy, dominated Africa's trade; as home markets filled up, protectionism replaced free trade and powers wanted colonies. Map 2.1 shows Africa mostly African-ruled in 1880 and almost all colonized by 1913.

am.text: አውሮፓውያን አፍሪካን ለገበያና ለጥሬ ዕቃ ፈለጉ፤ የብሔራዊ ኩራትና የኃይል ሚዛን ፍርሃትም ገፋፋቸው። በ1913 ከኢትዮጵያና ላይቤሪያ በስተቀር አፍሪካ ተያዘች።

screens.ask: In 1880 most of Africa was still ruled by Africans. How much do you think was under European rule by 1913?
screens.after: Map 2.1: in just 33 years almost the whole continent was partitioned.

screens.title: Why Europe scrambled
paras: Europe had industrialized for a century; it was the most powerful continent.
Firearms, transport and communication improved fast.

fear that rivals would grow stronger

paras: Britain dominated Africa's external trade until the later 1800s.
It had the largest merchant navy.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Scramble for Africa
The rush of European powers to claim African land, slow in the 1870s and fastest after 1885.
Protectionism
Protecting a country's own trade and markets instead of free trade, for example by holding colonies.
Colonialism
The rule of one country over another people and land, to control and use them.

screens.text: Which was an ECONOMIC motive for colonizing Africa?
opts: Fear for the balance of power
screens.why: Markets and raw materials were the economic motives; pride and balance of power were political.
screens.clue: Which one is about buying and selling?

screens.title: Economic or political motive?
screens.why: Money, goods and supplies are economic; pride and rivalry between states are political.
screens.clue: Is it about money or about power?

screens.text: Why could Britain set up trading stations and coastal colonies early?
opts: It was the leading industrial nation with the largest merchant navy
Africans asked Britain to rule them
screens.ans: It was the leading industrial nation with the largest merchant navy
screens.clue: Think of factories and ships.

screens.text: When their home markets became saturated, European powers moved from free trade toward protectionism.
screens.why: p.32: protectionism was encouraged more than free trade, and powers wanted colonies.
screens.clue: Full markets at home: where do you sell?

screens.text: Why did Britain and France build bigger African empires than Germany and Italy?
opts: They industrialized and arrived earlier, with strong navies and coastal bases
Germany and Italy did not want colonies
Africans preferred British and French rule
Germany and Italy had no armies
screens.ans: They industrialized and arrived earlier, with strong navies and coastal bases
screens.why: Germany and Italy united only in the early 1870s; by then there were few territories left to take.
screens.clue: Who arrived first?

screens.text: France fears that Britain will gain new colonies and grow stronger, so France rushes to claim land too. Which motive is this, and what did it cause?
opts: Balance of power; a competitive rush for African land
Raw materials; the end of colonies
screens.ans: Balance of power; a competitive rush for African land
screens.why: Fear that rivals would upset the balance of power turned slow claims into a race after 1885.
screens.clue: It is about rivals, not goods.

en.text: In 1884 Bismarck declared German protectorates over Togoland, Cameroon and South-West Africa, then invited the powers to Berlin. The conference (November 1884 – February 1885) settled Congo and Niger rivalries: Leopold II got the Congo Free State, the Congo Basin got free trade and the Niger free navigation. Its General Act made powers notify each other of claims and required "effective occupation". No African state, not even Ethiopia or Liberia, was invited, and the rush to occupy land followed.

am.text: በ1884–85 ቢስማርክ የበርሊን ጉባኤን ጠራ። ኮንጎ ለንጉሥ ሊዮፖልድ ተሰጠ፤ መሬት ለመያዝ ማሳወቅና "ውጤታማ ይዞታ" ያስፈልግ ነበር። ምንም የአፍሪካ አገር አልተጋበዘም።

screens.title: A meeting about Africa
screens.ask: In 1884–85 the powers met in Berlin to make rules for taking Africa. How many African states do you think were invited?
screens.after: None. Africa was the main agenda, but no African state, not even Ethiopia or Liberia, was invited.

screens.title: Why Berlin?
paras: Germany came late to Africa.
In 1884 Bismarck declared three German protectorates:
Togoland, Cameroon and South-West Africa (Namibia).
He then invited the powers to Berlin.
Aim 1: settle Congo claims of Britain, France and Portugal.
Aim 2: settle Anglo-French rivalry on the Niger River.

screens.title: The conference
paras: Held in Berlin, November 1884 – February 1885.
Called by Bismarck, the German chancellor.
14 states took part: European powers, the Ottoman Empire and the USA.
No African state was invited.
It added international agreement to a carving-up already under way.
The General Act was signed on 26 February 1885.
screens.note: The book says 13 European countries took part and the Ottoman Empire was absent; see the teacher note.

screens.title: What was decided
paras: The two key rules of the General Act:
Notify the other powers of every claim (Article 34).
Then occupy the land effectively, or the claim is invalid (Article 35).
table: the Congo Free State, his personal kingdom
lost most of its Congo claims
free trade in the Congo Basin; free navigation on the Niger

screens.title: Key words
defs: Berlin Conference
The meeting of powers in Berlin (November 1884 – February 1885) that set rules for claiming African land.
Protectorate
A territory that a stronger power declares it "protects" and in fact controls.
Effective occupation
The Berlin rule that a claim to African land was valid only if the power really occupied it.

screens.text: Who called the Berlin Conference?
screens.why: p.32: the German chancellor initiated it.
screens.clue: He was the leader of Germany.

Competitive rush to occupy African land (after 1885)

screens.clue: The rush came after the rules.

screens.text: The rule of "effective occupation" meant
opts: a claim was valid only if the power really occupied the land
Africans had to agree to colonial rule
only Germany could take new land
the powers had to leave Africa
screens.ans: a claim was valid only if the power really occupied the land
screens.why: p.33: "effective occupation" was needed for a claim to remain valid.
screens.clue: Drawing a line on a map was not enough.

screens.text: Why did the Berlin Conference speed up the conquest of Africa instead of slowing it?
opts: Claims needed effective occupation, so powers rushed to occupy land by force
It banned all trade in Africa
It gave all of Africa to Germany
It invited Africans to rule themselves
screens.ans: Claims needed effective occupation, so powers rushed to occupy land by force
screens.why: To keep a claim a power had to notify others and then occupy it, so each rushed to conquer before its rivals.
screens.clue: What did a power have to do to keep a claim?

notes.text: p.33: the book says 13 European countries attended (listing Austria and Hungary separately) and that the Ottoman Empire was not represented. In fact 14 states took part: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Denmark, France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Sweden-Norway, the Ottoman Empire and the USA. The lesson teaches 14; exams may still use the book's "13 European countries". No African state was invited (correct).

p.33: the General Act was signed on 26 February 1885 (book: 25 February). The notification duty is Article 34 and effective occupation is Article 35 (book: Article 36). The lesson teaches the corrected numbers.
p.31 "entre African continent" = entire. p.32: the printed sentence stops at "the new industrial powers"; read "... to establish colonies or 'protected' areas in Africa".
Activity 2.1 Q2 is used as a practice item (model answer from the transcription). "Highest stage of capitalism" is the book's (Lenin's) phrase and is quoted as the book's view.
